questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Career opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I am interested in a future career involving Japanese relations and GSAPS at Waseda had a reputation for good academic quality as well as academically active professors in fields I found interesting. Additionally, it was possible to participate in Japanese language classes outside of my major. As such, it seemed like a good match.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: There was a lot of information distributed through e-mail to us. I almost had a hard time because there was too much information coming out way. But I guess that is just part of going on exchange, especially outside of EU.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There were some orientation videos and materials as well as an online meeting. However, there was no offline meeting to help and introduce exchange students to each other. This might be a post-corona thing, but I thought it was strange that there was not physical orientation specifically for exchange students. So, lots of help for practical stuff, but very little social support. It was fine for me as I had contacts and friends in Tokyo already. But might be hard for others who come over to Tokyo for the first time.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
It was fairly easy, I would say. Much easier than Copenhagen! I feared the worst, but I actually just found it once I landed here. I had booked some showings prior to landing and then said yes to the place I liked the best. If landing in a foreign city without a home is not your thing, online showing are also possible in many places if you ask them for it. 

I lived in a small sharehouse I found through the website tokyosharehouse. I speak conversational Japanese so I lived in a Japanese speaking flat. If you're also interested in a sharehouse, things to look for are the ratio between the number of residents and toilets/baths, the size of the rooms, what year the building is from etc.. Higher floors are also referable as there are roaches in Tokyo in summer (seeing at least one is not uncommon), but the higher you are, the less they stop by. Also, go for places not too far from a well-connected station. Check the prices and be critical, sometimes the prices for sharehouses for foreigners can be a bit overpriced - sometimes it might even be almost the same as renting out a small flat for yourself.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Sometimes it might be a good thing. You can choose your own neighborhood! Look up what vibe different parts of Tokyo have.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The non-dormitory housing available through Waseda was not the best and I managed to find something on my own that was better (I would say).

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: There are multiple rounds, so you can add and drop. So if a course was over-enrolled and you did not get it, you could pick something else. You can even try some of the classes and then decide. However, at the grad school, I got all my selected courses.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I am not sure, I did not need more than the available material.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all my courses at the grad school. It was harder to get a place in Japanese classes.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Be sure to check the schedule for each course and make a study plan with no overlaps. 
Also, some courses are intense courses, where you study double for half the semester. Don't do too many of those, but one (maybe two) might be good since your exams will then be distributed throughout the semester.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: It depended on the Professor. So I would check out each professor's profile before and then choose. Most courses were easier than UCPH but some were just as challenging.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Much smaller classes, and a lot of classroom discussions with more interaction with the professor.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.answer: EU-Japan relations w. Professor Bacon. The professor is very knowledgeable and well-connected in the field. Expects participation from students.

questions.answer: A visit to the hospital!

questions.answer: I ended up having to go to the hospital and feared I had to pay a huge bill even if my Danish insurance later covered it. However, it was much less expensive than expected!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I did not participate so I do not know

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are many hobby clubs but mostly used by undergrads

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I did not participate.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: There are many good day trips from Tokyo to get out of the city such as Enoshima.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I had experience with living in Japan before but Tokyo was the first. I never got used to the crowds, but preferred more quiet neighborhoods like Koenji or Kichijoji.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: There are language exchange programs at the university, which seemed like a good way to make friends interested in an international outlook. Especially since many do not speak English.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Japanese are very hesitant and a bit hard to get close to at first. However, many are curious once you break the ice.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: There is usually great service and hospitality here, which makes it a good experience when you are exploring places and the city.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Look through the professors and choose courses based on their profiles. The academic level is manageable. As such, remember to explore the city, culture, and people instead of being too nervous about the academic stuff.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: The trains stop running around 00:00, beware!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: It was networking with other academics with similar interests as mine and building a new network here.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Choosing where to go for trips!

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: No

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
